title: Charing Cross — Fogg's newest London
learning_goal: Know that Fogg's London was brand-new (station 8, Underground 9, Embankment 2, Big Ben 13) and remember the twenty guineas; feel awe at a new city and one warm beat.

narration.script: The Strand, and ahead the forecourt of Charing Cross. Forget olde-worlde London: this was Fogg's newest London. The station had opened in January 1864 — eight years old that night. The hotel behind the cross, 1865. The cross itself, 1865. The Underground, nine years old. The Embankment down by the river, two. Big Ben — the clock tower — thirteen. So much of what Fogg passes tonight is younger than his valet. You cannot see it from here — Hawkshaw's roof, a single iron span about 155 metres by 50 — five hundred feet long — collapsed in 1905 and was replaced; that is all we will say about it. Then the one warm beat of the evening. At the station a barefoot woman with a child asks for money, and Fogg hands her the twenty guineas he won at whist. Without breaking stride. Four hundred and twenty shillings — about eight hundred and forty cab-miles.

production_notes: Roof dimensions are a conversion of F-21's 510 × 164 ft (≈ 155 × 50 m). The 1864 roof is gone (1905, replaced; Embankment Place sits over the platforms) and the train-shed is not visible from the Strand — hence 'You cannot see it from here'. The 1905 collapse gets one line, no drama (brief: no disaster tourism). 'So much of what Fogg passes' (not 'almost everything' — Trafalgar Square and St Martin's are older). First mention 'Big Ben — the clock tower', then 'the clock tower' (Continuity #21). Narrator: short sentences at the beggar-woman beat (Continuity #10). Linear cut: keep whole (60 s: 40 s video + 20 s M-51 still).
